capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user

inputs.source: user prompt in the desktop client
issue opened by any GitHub account in the public repository

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: PAT scope + user prompt
instructions.note: The user's request only concerns reading open issues in the public repo, but the single GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN configured for the MCP server carries repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private. Nothing in the configuration or task narrows the credential or the agent's reachable tools to match the stated task.

controls.name: Per-tool-call human approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The gate is enforced by the client outside the model, but arguments are collapsed by default, so the approver sees a summary rather than the raw destination and payload. A more persuasive model can shape that summary, and the stated pattern of approving many calls per session is the volume condition that drives approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Repository-scoped least-privilege token excluding private repos
controls.decay_rationale: A token that cannot read private repositories removes the sensitive data from the reachable set entirely; this does not decay with model capability because the model cannot use access it does not have.

controls.name: Raw action approval review for get_file_contents and create_pull_request
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the full repository target and diff removes the summarization step a stronger model can exploit, though it still depends on the human reading it correctly.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) via confused deputy (TC4): a malicious public issue drives private-repo read and public-PR exfiltration

attack_path.note: Anyone on GitHub can open an issue in the public repo; its text is untrusted (U) content that enters the agent's context when it 'looks at open issues'.

The issue instructs the agent to fetch confidential content from a private repository; this is reachable only because the shared PAT is scoped broadly across all repos, public and private (confused deputy, TC4).
The agent opens a pull request on the public repo carrying the private content, an irreversible egress visible to the issue's author and anyone else with access to the public repo.

forecast.watch_signal: Approval volume per session rising (approval fatigue), the client switching to an auto-approve or 'agent mode' setting, model upgrade making collapsed-argument summaries more persuasive or selectively incomplete, or any config change that removes/narrows the per-call prompt.

evidence.observation: A single GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN is passed to the MCP server with no scope restriction expressed in the client config.
The PAT has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so cap.read_private_repo and cap.create_pr_public share one broad credential (credential_scope: broad).
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making in.public_issue an untrusted (U) source reachable by any external actor with no authentication to the principal.

Approval is required per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session — a model_summary review mode, which is partially_dependent and subject to approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).
The user only asked to look at open issues in the public repo; nothing authorizes reading private repos or opening a PR, yet the agent's credential and toolset permit both in the same session.

recommendations.action: Issue a repository-scoped, least-privilege token (fine-grained PAT or GitHub App installation token) limited to the public repo for sessions like this one; never configure a single MCP server instance with an account-wide token spanning private repositories unless the task requires it.

Change the approval prompt to raw_action review mode: expand arguments by default so the approver sees the full source repo, destination repo, and diff for get_file_contents and create_pull_request before approving, rather than a collapsed summary.

Add a destination confirmation bound to the system of record so create_pull_request cannot target a different repository than the one the user named, and so content sourced from a private-repo read cannot be included in a PR opened against a public repo without an explicit, separate reconfirmation step.

Log and alert when a single session both reads a private repository and writes to a public one (a cross-sensitivity data flow), so the pattern is caught even when a human approves each individual call.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted public GitHub issue (U) can drive a path that reads confidential private-repo content and then egresses it irreversibly via a public pull request (S3), and the shared account-wide PAT means no credential boundary separates the two repos. The only present control is a per-tool-call human approval prompt; because its arguments are collapsed by default and the design expects many approvals per session, it is scored as a structural but partially_dependent (model_summary) gate. Applying the rubric's -2 tier credit for an approval gate, capped at a floor of moderate because the review is not raw_action, yields a residual of moderate. No scoped credential, egress allowlist, or destination-binding control is declared, so nothing severs the path (step 1 does not apply) and no independent narrowing controls apply at step 3. Forecast: under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or any control_removal that disables or bypasses the per-call prompt (including simple approval fatigue from high call volume, SAFE-T1403), the only credited control fails, returning the finding to its critical inherent tier. The single control whose decay most moves the forecast is ctl.tool_call_prompt.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as provided (the MCP client config and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or agent instructions were supplied beyond the user's one-line request, so the review of instruction issues is limited to what is inferable from the stated task and the credential/tool configuration.

Details of the docker container's sandboxing (network egress rules, filesystem mounts, outbound destination restrictions) were not provided, so no containment credit beyond the credential itself was given; this is a confidence gap, not a claim that no sandboxing exists.

The exact GitHub token model (classic PAT vs. fine-grained PAT vs. GitHub App installation token) was not specified beyond 'repo scope across every repository the user owns', so credential_scope is inferred as broad/shared rather than verified against a token's actual permission list.
